title: One Penguin Colony Holds Steady While Its Neighbor Shrinks
summary:
Two groups of rare penguins live on remote islands near New Zealand, and their fortunes could hardly be more different. One colony has held steady for at least 25 years. The other has shrunk by more than 40 percent.

The birds are Erect-crested penguins, and they breed nowhere else on Earth except the Bounty and Antipodes islands, about 800 kilometres southeast of New Zealand's South Island. A new study from the University of Otago, published in the journal PLOS ONE, used drone surveys between 2022 and 2024 to count every breeding colony across both island groups.

The results surprised the researchers. The tiny Bounty Islands, covering just 50 hectares, hold about 27,800 breeding pairs — almost as many as the Antipodes Islands, with about 29,800 pairs, even though the Antipodes are 40 times larger and were long thought to be the species' stronghold.

Comparing the new counts with records going back to the mid-1990s, the Bounty population has stayed essentially unchanged for at least 25 years. The Antipodes population, by contrast, has declined by more than 40 percent since 1995.

Scientists think several pressures may be behind the split. One is the skua, a native subantarctic bird that preys on penguin eggs and chicks. As colonies shrink, the birds lose some of the safety that comes from nesting together in large numbers, so predation losses can grow and colonies can fragment further.

Another factor may involve Eastern Rockhopper penguins, which suffered a severe population collapse in the second half of the 20th century. Fewer than 1,000 breeding pairs remain on the Antipodes Islands today. As Rockhoppers disappeared, skuas may have turned to Erect-crested penguin eggs and chicks instead. Stronger storms have also caused landslides that break up breeding colonies and leave the birds more vulnerable.
why_it_matters: The split between two nearby colonies shows how fast a rare species can decline, and understanding why helps scientists protect the penguins before the losses spread.

background_read: Erect-crested penguins breed only on two small island groups near New Zealand, the Bounty and Antipodes islands, so their whole future depends on what happens there.
Penguins nest in large colonies, and nesting close together helps protect eggs and chicks from hunters like the skua, a seabird that eats them.
When a colony shrinks, that shared protection weakens, and losses can grow.
Scientists count breeding pairs with drone surveys to track whether each colony is holding steady or shrinking over time.

KEY EVENT: A drone survey counted every breeding colony on the Bounty and Antipodes islands.

├─ WHEN: Surveys ran between 2022 and 2024; counts were compared with records back to the mid-1990s
